header: ENERGY AND WATER DEVELOPMENT AND RELATED AGENCIES APPROPRIATIONS ACT, 2016
summary:
This division funds the Army Corps of Engineers’ civil works, the Interior Department’s western water programs, most of the Department of Energy, and several related independent agencies for fiscal year 2016. Its purpose is to pay for harbors, flood protection, dams and irrigation, energy research, nuclear weapons work and cleanup, federal hydropower marketing, and nuclear safety regulation.

## Total Spending

The division does not print one official grand total. Adding the appropriation lines in the text comes to about **$39.0 billion** before offsets and small rescissions:

- **Army Corps of Engineers (Title I):** $5.99 billion
- **Interior / Bureau of Reclamation (Title II):** $1.28 billion
- **Department of Energy, including nuclear security and cleanup (Title III):** about $30.5 billion
- **Independent agencies (Title IV):** about $1.22 billion

A large share does not come straight from general taxpayers. Harbor and inland-waterway trust funds, the Reclamation Fund, the Uranium Enrichment Decontamination and Decommissioning Fund, and the Nuclear Waste Fund cover parts of the bill. Power-sale revenues offset most Power Marketing Administration costs. Licensing fees cover almost all of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission and most of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission. No prior-year comparison was provided with the text.

## Key Funding Areas

- **NNSA Weapons Activities**: $8.85 billion — maintains and updates the U.S. nuclear weapons stockpile and related facilities.
- **Department of Energy Science**: $5.35 billion — basic research at national labs and universities, including not more than $115 million for the international ITER fusion project.
- **Defense Environmental Cleanup**: $5.29 billion — cleans up contamination from nuclear weapons production.
- **Corps Operation and Maintenance**: $3.14 billion — keeps existing harbors, channels, locks, flood-control works, and related infrastructure operating; part is paid from the Harbor Maintenance Trust Fund.
- **Energy Efficiency and Renewable Energy**: $2.07 billion — research and development on energy efficiency and renewable energy; up to $45 million may be transferred to the Defense Production Act Fund.
- **Defense Nuclear Nonproliferation**: $1.94 billion — programs to keep nuclear weapons and materials from spreading.
- **Corps Construction**: $1.86 billion — builds authorized navigation, flood and storm protection, shore protection, and aquatic ecosystem projects. The federal share of some inland waterway work comes from the Inland Waterways Trust Fund.
- **Naval Reactors**: $1.38 billion — nuclear propulsion work for Navy ships and submarines.
- **Bureau of Reclamation, Water and Related Resources**: $1.12 billion — operates, maintains, and rehabilitates western water projects and related tribal and local partnerships.
- **Nuclear Regulatory Commission**: $990 million — regulates civilian nuclear power and materials. Fees are expected to cover about $873 million, leaving an estimated $117 million from the general fund. A separate inspector general account is $12.1 million, mostly fee-funded.

Other notable lines include Nuclear Energy at $986 million, Other Defense Activities at $776 million, uranium enrichment cleanup at $674 million (from a dedicated fund), Fossil Energy Research and Development at $632 million, the Mississippi River and Tributaries account at $345 million, the Strategic Petroleum Reserve at $212 million, the Corps regulatory program at $200 million, and the Appalachian Regional Commission at $146 million.

## Notable Provisions

- The Corps may start no more than **10 new studies** (7 mainly for navigation or flood and storm protection, 3 mainly for environmental restoration) and **6 new construction projects** (5 navigation or flood and storm protection, 1 environmental restoration). It must show Congress an out-year funding plan before new construction starts are treated as final, and it may not later deviate from the submitted work plan.
- One percent of each Corps operation-and-maintenance item is held back until the fourth quarter for emergencies.
- Up to $5.4 million may be transferred from Corps operation and maintenance to the Fish and Wildlife Service to offset fisheries lost because of Corps projects.
- The Corps may not, in fiscal year 2016, change the October 1, 2012, regulatory definitions of “fill material” or “discharge of fill material” under the Clean Water Act.
- Open-lake disposal of dredged material from Lake Erie or its tributaries is barred unless a state water-quality certification approves it.
- Funds may not be used to require Clean Water Act dredge-or-fill permits for certain farming and maintenance activities already listed as exemptions in the statute.
- The Ten Mile Creek Water Preserve Area project in Florida is to be transferred to the South Florida Water Management District and will no longer be a federal project.
- The Reclamation Safety of Dams Act is amended so extra project benefits, such as added water storage, can be built during dam-safety work if nonfederal partners share the cost. The dam-safety authorization ceiling is increased by **$1.1 billion** (in October 2003 prices). That is permission to spend later, not new cash in this bill. The size of a modification that needs a formal report to Congress is raised from $1.25 million to $20 million.
- The Secure Water Act authorization ceiling rises from $300 million to $350 million. CALFED Bay-Delta authorization is extended from 2016 to 2017. Deadlines are set for several California water feasibility studies.
- The Energy Secretary must report by May 2, 2016, on whether the United States should stay in ITER after October 2017 or leave, including the estimated cost of either choice.
- New Defense Nuclear Nonproliferation contracts or assistance agreements with the Russian Federation are barred unless the Secretary personally waives the ban for national security and notifies Congress.
- No new regional petroleum-product reserve may be created unless Congress is asked for the money in a budget request and approves it in an appropriations act.
- Funds may not be used to enforce certain federal efficiency standards for specified incandescent reflector lamps (BPAR, BR, and ER lamps) or the standard in 10 CFR 430.32(x).
- At least $160 million tied to earlier clean-coal and FutureGen selections that have not reached financial close must be shifted to previously selected demonstration projects that have.
- High-hazard nuclear construction needs independent safety oversight, and projects over $100 million need an independent cost estimate before major construction decisions.
- Small prior-year balances are rescinded, including $19.9 million from National Nuclear Security Administration federal salaries and expenses and a few million dollars from older energy-efficiency and science accounts.
- Regional development agencies receive $146 million for Appalachia, $25 million for the Delta Regional Authority, $11 million for the Denali Commission in Alaska, $7.5 million for the Northern Border Regional Commission, and $250,000 for the Southeast Crescent Regional Commission. Denali’s federal share may be up to 80 percent in distressed communities and 50 percent elsewhere.
- A narrow Alaska provision allows certain funds to be used for barge mooring points and landing sites so fuel can be pumped from barges into bulk storage tanks.
- Across the division, agencies generally cannot start, stop, or sharply reshuffle programs without notice to, and in many cases approval from, the Appropriations Committees. Funds may not be used to lobby Congress, and they may not be used in violation of the 1994 environmental-justice executive order.

## Who Benefits

- Port, shipping, and river communities that depend on dredged channels, locks, and flood works, including the Mississippi River valley and coastal harbors.
- Western farmers, cities, tribes, and ecosystems served by Bureau of Reclamation dams and water projects, with specific funding for the Central Valley Project, California Bay-Delta, and the Central Utah Project.
- National laboratories, university researchers, and energy-technology developers working on science, efficiency, renewables, nuclear energy, fossil energy, and grid reliability.
- Workers and nearby communities at former nuclear-weapons and uranium-enrichment sites receiving cleanup money.
- The Navy, through naval reactors, and the broader nuclear-security enterprise.
- Customers of federal hydropower marketed by the Bonneville, Southeastern, Southwestern, and Western area power administrations.
- People in Appalachia, the Mississippi Delta, Alaska, the northern border region, and the Southeast crescent, through regional commissions.
- Nuclear plant operators and the public, through Nuclear Regulatory Commission oversight that is largely paid for by industry fees.

## Plain English Summary

This is the 2016 check for water projects and a big part of the Energy Department. The largest pieces keep the nuclear weapons complex running, pay scientists at the national labs, and clean up old nuclear sites. Another large share goes to the Army Corps of Engineers to dredge harbors, maintain locks and levees, and build a limited number of new flood, navigation, and restoration projects. The Bureau of Reclamation gets a bit over a billion dollars for western water supply. There is also about $2 billion for energy efficiency and renewables, plus smaller amounts for nuclear energy research, fossil energy research, the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, and regional economic commissions from Appalachia to Alaska. Congress kept a tight leash on new Corps projects, blocked a few regulatory changes, restricted new nonproliferation deals with Russia, and required a decision path on whether the United States stays in a major international fusion project.

## Title Summary

Title I funds the Army Corps of Engineers’ civil works program under the Department of the Army for fiscal year 2016. It covers investigations, construction, and operation and maintenance of river and harbor, flood and storm damage reduction, shore protection, and aquatic ecosystem restoration projects, plus the Mississippi River and Tributaries program, wetlands and navigable-waters regulation, cleanup of early atomic-energy sites (FUSRAP), flood and coastal emergency preparedness, and Corps civil-works administration. Appropriations in the title total **$5,989,000,000**.

## Spending Breakdown

| Line Item | Amount | Purpose |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| Investigations | $121,000,000 | Surveys, studies, and plans for proposed navigation, flood, shore, and ecosystem projects; up to 10 new study starts |
| Construction | $1,862,250,000 | Construction of authorized civil works projects; up to six new construction starts; federal shares drawn as needed from the Harbor Maintenance Trust Fund and Inland Waterways Trust Fund |
| Mississippi River and Tributaries | $345,000,000 | Flood damage reduction in the Mississippi River alluvial valley below Cape Girardeau, Missouri |
| Operation and Maintenance | $3,137,000,000 | Operation, maintenance, and security of existing projects; harbor channels, charting, and navigation obstructions; eligible costs from the Harbor Maintenance Trust Fund and related fee accounts |
| Regulatory Program | $200,000,000 | Administration of laws regulating navigable waters and wetlands (available through Sept. 30, 2017) |
| Formerly Utilized Sites Remedial Action Program | $112,000,000 | Cleanup of contamination from the Nation’s early atomic energy program |
| Flood Control and Coastal Emergencies | $28,000,000 | Preparedness and emergency response for floods, hurricanes, and other natural disasters |
| Expenses | $179,000,000 | Civil works supervision and administration, including research, water resources, and finance support activities (through Sept. 30, 2017); no more than $5,000 for reception and representation |
| Office of the Assistant Secretary of the Army for Civil Works | $4,750,000 | Office of the Assistant Secretary (through Sept. 30, 2017) |

## Notable Sections

- **New-start caps.** Investigations may begin no more than 10 new studies (seven navigation or flood/storm, three environmental restoration). Construction may begin no more than six new projects (five navigation or flood/storm, one environmental restoration). Cost-sharing agreements for new construction must be executed by August 31, 2016, and out-year affordability must be shown to the Appropriations Committees before allocations are final. The Secretary may not deviate from new starts in the submitted work plan.
- **Work-plan hold.** No more than 50 percent of the Assistant Secretary’s appropriation may be obligated until a work plan allocates at least 95 percent of additional funding under each heading to specific programs, projects, or activities.
- **Reprogramming limits (Sec. 101).** Funds may not be reprogrammed to create, eliminate, or redirect projects beyond set percentage and dollar caps without Appropriations Committee approval. Operation and maintenance has unlimited reprogramming for emergencies, with notice to the committees. One percent of each O&M program is withheld until the fourth quarter for emergency use by the Chief of Engineers.
- **Contracting limit (Sec. 103).** Contracts may not commit funds beyond unobligated amounts for that activity, except funds available through Sec. 101 reprogramming.
- **Fisheries transfer (Sec. 104).** Up to **$5,400,000** of Operation and Maintenance funds may be transferred to the Fish and Wildlife Service to mitigate fisheries losses from Corps projects.
- **Clean Water Act restrictions (Secs. 105 and 110).** Funds may not be used in FY2016 to change the October 1, 2012, regulatory definitions of “fill material” or “discharge of fill material.” Funds also may not be used to require a dredged- or fill-material permit for activities already identified in Clean Water Act section 404(f)(1)(A) and (C).
- **Lake Erie dredging (Sec. 106).** Open-lake placement of dredged material from Lake Erie or its tributaries is barred unless approved under a state water-quality certification.
- **Project transfer (Sec. 107).** Within 180 days, the Secretary must transfer the Ten Mile Creek Water Preserve Area Critical Restoration Project to the South Florida Water Management District for environmental restoration, water storage, and treatment; it then ceases to be a federal project.
- **Other limits.** Acquisitions must comply with 48 CFR 225.7007 (Sec. 108). Funds may not continue the Corps study under section 5018(a)(1) of the Water Resources Development Act of 2007 (Sec. 109). Allocations must follow this Act and the accompanying explanatory statement (Sec. 102).

## Plain English

This title pays the Army Corps of Engineers to study, build, and maintain harbors, waterways, flood protections, and ecosystem projects, regulate wetlands and navigable waters, and clean up old atomic-energy sites.

## Title Summary

Title II funds the Department of the Interior’s water-resources work in this Energy and Water division: the Central Utah Project Completion Account and the Bureau of Reclamation. It covers operation, maintenance, and rehabilitation of reclamation facilities; water and habitat restoration (including Central Valley Project and California Bay-Delta activities); related work with states, local governments, and Indian tribes; and Bureau policy and administration. Appropriations under the main accounts total **$1,275,000,000**.

## Spending Breakdown

| Line Item | Amount | Purpose |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| Central Utah Project Completion Account | $10,000,000 | Activities under the Central Utah Project Completion Act (available until expended). |
| — of which, Utah Reclamation Mitigation and Conservation Account | $1,000,000 | Deposit for use by the Utah Reclamation Mitigation and Conservation Commission. |
| — of which, Secretary of the Interior expenses | $1,350,000 | Related Interior responsibilities; available until September 30, 2017. |
| Water and Related Resources | $1,118,972,000 | Management, development, and restoration of water and related resources; facility O&M and rehabilitation; Native American responsibilities; grants and agreements (available until expended). |
| — of which, Upper Colorado River Basin Fund | $22,000 | Transfer to that fund. |
| — of which, Lower Colorado River Basin Development Fund | $5,899,000 | Transfer to that fund. |
| Central Valley Project Restoration Fund | $49,528,000 | Habitat restoration, improvement, and acquisition under the Central Valley Project Improvement Act; derived from restoration-fund collections. |
| California Bay-Delta Restoration | $37,000,000 | Activities under the Water Supply, Reliability, and Environmental Improvement Act, including the federal share of CALFED program management; transfers to other federal agencies allowed. |
| Policy and Administration | $59,500,000 | Commissioner’s office, Denver office, and five regional offices; from the Reclamation Fund, available until September 30, 2017; nonreimbursable. |
| Administrative provision | No dollar amount | Purchase of up to five replacement passenger motor vehicles. |

The Commission may also use up to **$1,500,000** of amounts otherwise available to it in FY2016 for administrative expenses. Program amounts that can be financed by the Reclamation Fund or the special fee account under 16 U.S.C. 6806 are to be derived from those sources. Youth Conservation Corps work on high-priority projects is authorized from Water and Related Resources.

## Notable Sections

- **Sec. 201** — Limits reprogramming of Water and Related Resources (including prior-year balances still available in FY2016). Bars creating, eliminating, restarting, or increasing denied or restricted projects without Appropriations Committee approval, and caps transfers (generally 15% or $300,000, depending on the activity’s size; $500,000 between major categories; $5,000,000 for certain legal obligations). Requires quarterly reprogramming reports.
- **Sec. 202** — Blocks use of funds to set the final discharge point for the San Luis Unit interceptor drain until Interior and California develop a plan meeting state water-quality standards approved by EPA. Classifies Kesterson cleanup and San Joaquin Valley drainage costs as reimbursable or nonreimbursable under 1995 repayment plans; future San Luis Unit drainage obligations are fully reimbursable by beneficiaries.
- **Sec. 203** — Amends the Reclamation Safety of Dams Act so the Secretary may add project benefits (including extra conservation storage) with dam-safety work if a cost-share agreement is reached and those costs are paid only by beneficiaries of the added benefits.
- **Sec. 204** — Raises the Safety of Dams construction ceiling by an additional **$1,100,000,000** (October 1, 2003 price levels), effective October 1, 2015. Raises the modification-notice threshold from $1,250,000 to **$20,000,000**, and requires 30-day written notice to the House Natural Resources and Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committees for modifications between $1,800,000 and $20,000,000.
- **Sec. 205** — Sets deadlines (December 31, 2015; November 30, 2016; December 31, 2017) for completing and submitting specified California water feasibility studies under Public Law 108–361, plus recurring progress reports.
- **Sec. 206** — Increases the Secure Water Act of 2009 authorization ceiling from $300,000,000 to **$350,000,000**.
- **Sec. 207** — Extends the CALFED Bay-Delta Authorization Act sunset from 2016 to **2017**.
- **CVP Restoration Fund proviso** — Prohibits using those funds to acquire or lease water for in-stream purposes if a court decree or order already commits that water to in-stream use. Directs Reclamation to assess and collect the full additional mitigation and restoration payments authorized by section 3407(d) of Public Law 102–575.

## Plain English

This title pays for federal dams, canals, and water projects run by the Bureau of Reclamation—especially in the West and California—plus finishing the Central Utah Project, while tightening how those funds can be shifted and expanding dam-safety authority.

**Title III — Department of Energy** (Division D; fiscal year 2016) funds DOE’s civilian energy programs, the National Nuclear Security Administration, defense nuclear cleanup, the power marketing administrations, and the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission.

## Title Summary

This title appropriates money for energy efficiency and renewable energy, grid reliability, nuclear and fossil R&D, the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, DOE science (including a capped U.S. contribution to ITER), ARPA-E, and loan-program administration. It also funds NNSA weapons activities, nuclear nonproliferation, and naval reactors, plus cleanup of defense and uranium-enrichment sites, and operation of the federal power marketing administrations and FERC. Most research, weapons, and cleanup accounts remain available until expended; several salary and administration accounts expire September 30, 2017.

## Spending Breakdown

Amounts below are the sums stated in each account. Program-direction figures are included in the parent amount, not added to it. Power-marketing and FERC totals are largely offset by collections or fees.

| Line Item | Amount | Purpose |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| Energy Efficiency and Renewable Energy | $2,073,000,000 | Efficiency and renewable energy activities, plant, and capital equipment; includes $155,000,000 for program direction. Up to $45,000,000 may be transferred to the Defense Production Act Fund. |
| Electricity Delivery and Energy Reliability | $206,000,000 | Grid delivery and reliability; includes $28,000,000 for program direction. |
| Nuclear Energy | $986,161,000 | Civilian nuclear energy activities; includes $80,000,000 for program direction. |
| Fossil Energy Research and Development | $632,000,000 | Fossil energy R&D, including extraction, processing, use, and disposal of mineral substances; includes $114,202,000 for program direction. |
| Naval Petroleum and Oil Shale Reserves | $17,500,000 | Naval petroleum and oil shale reserve activities; prior-year unobligated balances also remain available. |
| Strategic Petroleum Reserve | $212,000,000 | SPR facility development, operations, and program management. |
| Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve | $7,600,000 | Storage, operation, and management of the Northeast reserve. |
| Energy Information Administration | $122,000,000 | Energy data collection and analysis. |
| Non-Defense Environmental Cleanup | $255,000,000 | Cleanup of non-defense DOE sites. |
| Uranium Enrichment D&D Fund | $673,749,000 | Decontamination and decommissioning of uranium enrichment facilities, derived from that Fund; $32,959,000 is for Energy Policy Act of 1992, title X, subtitle A activities. |
| Science | $5,350,200,000 | DOE Office of Science, including facilities and up to 17 replacement passenger vehicles; includes $185,000,000 for program direction. Not more than $115,000,000 for ITER in-kind contributions and related support. |
| ARPA-E | $291,000,000 | Advanced Research Projects Agency–Energy; includes $29,250,000 for program direction. |
| Title 17 Loan Guarantee Program (admin.) | $42,000,000 | Administrative expenses. $25,000,000 in borrower fees is credited as offsetting collections, so the estimated general-fund cost is not more than $17,000,000. Credit subsidy is limited to amounts collected from borrowers under prior law. |
| Advanced Technology Vehicles Manufacturing Loan Program | $6,000,000 | Administrative expenses only. |
| Departmental Administration | $248,142,000 | DOE salaries and expenses; includes $31,297,000 for Energy Policy and Systems Analysis. Estimated miscellaneous revenues of $117,171,000 reduce the estimated general-fund cost to not more than $130,971,000. |
| Office of the Inspector General | $46,424,000 | DOE Inspector General. |
| **NNSA — Weapons Activities** | **$8,846,948,000** | Nuclear weapons activities; includes $97,118,000 for program direction. Funds may be used for project engineering and design of the Albuquerque Complex Project. |
| **NNSA — Defense Nuclear Nonproliferation** | **$1,940,302,000** | Defense nuclear nonproliferation. |
| **NNSA — Naval Reactors** | **$1,375,496,000** | Naval nuclear propulsion; includes $42,504,000 for program direction. |
| **NNSA — Federal Salaries and Expenses** | **$383,666,000** | NNSA federal salaries and expenses. Separately, $19,900,000 in prior-year unobligated balances under this heading is rescinded. |
| Defense Environmental Cleanup | $5,289,742,000 | Cleanup of atomic-energy defense sites; includes $281,951,000 for program direction. Allows purchase of one replacement fire pumper and one replacement armored vehicle. |
| Other Defense Activities | $776,425,000 | Other atomic-energy defense and classified activities; includes $249,137,000 for program direction. |
| Bonneville Power Administration Fund | No new appropriation | Approves specified BPA Fund expenditures (including three tribal/hatchery projects). No new direct loan obligations in FY2016. Reception expenses capped at $5,000. |
| Southeastern Power Administration | $6,900,000 | Transmission O&M and power marketing. Fully offset by power-sale collections; estimated final appropriation $0. Up to $66,500,000 more in collections may cover purchase-power and wheeling costs. |
| Southwestern Power Administration | $47,361,000 | Transmission O&M, marketing, and construction. After up to $35,961,000 in offsetting collections, estimated net appropriation is not more than $11,400,000. Up to $63,000,000 more may cover purchase-power and wheeling. |
| Western Area Power Administration | $307,714,000 | Construction, rehabilitation, O&M, and conservation/renewable programs; $302,000,000 derived from the Reclamation Fund. After up to $214,342,000 in offsetting collections, estimated net appropriation is not more than $93,372,000 ($87,658,000 of that from the Reclamation Fund). Up to $352,813,000 more may cover purchase-power and wheeling. |
| Falcon and Amistad O&M Fund | $4,490,000 | Hydro O&M and emergency costs at Falcon and Amistad Dams, from that Fund. After up to $4,262,000 in offsetting collections, estimated net appropriation is not more than $228,000. WAPA may accept up to $460,000 from U.S. power customers. |
| Federal Energy Regulatory Commission | $319,800,000 | FERC salaries and expenses, retained from fees and annual charges. Estimated general-fund appropriation is $0. |
| Sec. 310 rescissions (prior balances) | $7,006,500.18 | Rescinds unobligated balances: EERE — $1,355,149.00 (P.L. 110–161), $627,299.24 (P.L. 111–8), and $1,824,051.94 (P.L. 111–85); Science — $3,200,000.00. |
| Sec. 313 reallocation (prior funds) | At least $160,000,000 | Prior Fossil Energy / Clean Coal Technology balances from projects that have not reached financial close must be shifted to previously selected demonstration projects that have. |

The account headings above sum to about **$30.47 billion** before the rescissions and before netting offsetting collections, fee revenue, and Fund/Reclamation Fund financing. That figure is a sum of the stated appropriations, not an official score of net general-fund cost.

## Notable Sections

- **ITER decision (Science):** Caps ITER support at $115,000,000 and requires the Secretary, by May 2, 2016, to recommend whether the United States stay in ITER after October 2017 or terminate participation, with a full future-cost estimate or a termination-cost estimate.
- **Sec. 307 — Russia:** Bars new Defense Nuclear Nonproliferation contracts or federal-assistance agreements with the Russian Federation. The Secretary may waive the ban for U.S. national security interests; the waiver cannot be delegated and takes effect only 15 days after a justification is sent to the Appropriations Committees.
- **Sec. 312 — lamp standards:** Prohibits use of funds in this Act to implement or enforce 10 C.F.R. § 430.32(x), or to implement or enforce statutory efficiency standards for BPAR, BR, and ER incandescent reflector lamps.
- **Sec. 313 — clean coal / FutureGen:** Requires at least $160,000,000 from stalled Clean Coal Power Initiative and FutureGen projects to be deobligated if needed and reallocated to demonstration projects that have reached financial close or otherwise secured construction funding. Federal aid for cost overruns may exceed the original cost share and is not limited to 25 percent of the original assistance. Must be implemented within 60 days of enactment.
- **Sec. 308 — regional product reserves:** The Secretary may not create a new regional petroleum product reserve unless the funding is requested in an annual budget and approved in an appropriations act, with justification, cost, operating plan, location, and inventory.
- **Loan guarantees:** Title 17 forbids subordinating a DOE loan obligation, or a guaranteed obligation, in violation of section 1702 of the Energy Policy Act

## Title Summary

Title IV funds several independent regional development commissions and nuclear oversight bodies for fiscal year 2016. It covers the Appalachian Regional Commission, Delta Regional Authority, Denali Commission, Northern Border Regional Commission, and Southeast Crescent Regional Commission, plus the Defense Nuclear Facilities Safety Board, Nuclear Regulatory Commission (including its Inspector General), and Nuclear Waste Technical Review Board. Most NRC spending is offset by licensing and inspection fees, so the net general appropriation is far below the gross figures.

## Spending Breakdown

| Line Item | Amount | Purpose |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| Appalachian Regional Commission | $146,000,000 | Programs under the Appalachian Regional Development Act of 1965; Federal Co-Chairman, Alternate, and Federal share of Commission administrative expenses; available until expended |
| Defense Nuclear Facilities Safety Board—Salaries and Expenses | $29,150,000 | Activities authorized by the Atomic Energy Act of 1954; available until September 30, 2017 |
| Delta Regional Authority—Salaries and Expenses | $25,000,000 | Authority activities under the Delta Regional Authority Act of 2000; available until expended |
| Denali Commission | $11,000,000 | Operating and capital expenses; Federal share of construction limited to 80% in distressed communities and 50% in non-distressed communities; available until expended |
| Northern Border Regional Commission | $7,500,000 | Activities under subtitle V of title 40, U.S.C., including administrative expenses; available until expended |
| Southeast Crescent Regional Commission | $250,000 | Activities under subtitle V of title 40, U.S.C.; available until expended |
| Nuclear Regulatory Commission—Salaries and Expenses | $990,000,000 gross; net estimated at not more than $117,136,000 after $872,864,000 in retained fee revenues | NRC operations under the Energy Reorganization Act of 1974 and the Atomic Energy Act of 1954; official representation capped at $25,000 |
| — of which, Office of the Commission support | not more than $7,500,000 | Salaries, travel, and support; spending requires a majority vote of the Commission; available until September 30, 2017 |
| — of which, university research and development | $10,000,000 | University R&D relevant to the NRC mission |
| — of which, Nuclear Science and Engineering Grant Program | $5,000,000 | Multiyear projects critical to maintaining nuclear science and engineering, even if not aligned with programmatic missions |
| Nuclear Regulatory Commission—Office of Inspector General | $12,136,000 gross; net estimated at not more than $2,076,000 after $10,060,000 in retained fee revenues | Inspector General Act activities; available until September 30, 2017 |
| — of which, IG services for the Defense Nuclear Facilities Safety Board | $958,000 | IG services for DNFSB; not available from fee revenues |
| Nuclear Waste Technical Review Board—Salaries and Expenses | $3,600,000 | Board expenses authorized by Public Law 100–203; derived from the Nuclear Waste Fund; available until September 30, 2017 |

## Notable Sections

- **Fee-funded NRC budget.** License, inspection, and service fees estimated at $872,864,000 (salaries and expenses) and $10,060,000 (Inspector General) are retained and used to reduce the final FY2016 appropriations to about $117,136,000 and $2,076,000, respectively.
- **Directed NRC set-asides.** Within the NRC account, $10,000,000 is for university R&D and $5,000,000 is for a Nuclear Science and Engineering Grant Program for work that may not match current programmatic missions.
- **Denali cost-share caps.** Construction aid is limited to 80% of project cost in distressed communities and 50% elsewhere.
- **Statutory waivers.** Several “notwithstanding” clauses let the Appalachian, Delta, Denali, and Northern Border commissions spend outside specified limits in their authorizing statutes, including on administration.
- **Sec. 401.** Requires the NRC to follow the July 5, 2011, version of Chapter VI of its Internal Commission Procedures when answering congressional information requests.
- **Sec. 402.** Allows NRC reprogramming, but requires 30-day notice to both Appropriations Committees for shifts above $500,000 or 10%, whichever is less; permits a health, environment, welfare, or national-security waiver with notice within 3 days; bars reprogramming that increases funds or personnel for activities this Act denies or restricts; and requires a monthly report of budget authority, unobligated balances, and unliquidated obligations.
- **Sec. 403.** Amends Public Law 105–277 so Denali Commission authority covers construction and repair of barge mooring points and landing sites used to pump fuel from barges into bulk storage tanks.

## Plain English

This title pays for regional economic-development commissions in Appalachia, the Delta, Alaska, the northern border, and the Southeast, and for nuclear-safety watchdogs, with most of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission’s budget covered by fees from the industry it regulates rather than by taxpayers.

## Title Summary

Title V sets government-wide conditions on how money appropriated in this Act may be used. It does not appropriate new funds. It bars lobbying of Congress with these funds (except ordinary communications allowed by 18 U.S.C. 1913), restricts transfers into and out of accounts funded in title III, and requires that none of the Act’s funds be used contrary to Executive Order 12898 on environmental justice.

## Spending Breakdown

| Line Item | Amount | Purpose |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| *(none)* | — | This title contains no appropriations or dollar amounts. It only imposes restrictions and a reporting requirement on funds provided elsewhere in the Act. |

## Notable Sections

- **Sec. 501 (anti-lobbying):** Prohibits using any funds in the Act, directly or indirectly, to influence congressional action on pending legislation or appropriations, other than communications to Members described in 18 U.S.C. 1913.
- **Sec. 502 (transfer limits):** Bars moving title III funds to other federal entities, and bars moving other agencies’ funds into title III accounts, except under transfer authority in this or another appropriations Act, authority cited in the explanatory statement referenced in section 4, or authority to provide goods or services between agencies. Agency heads who use transfer authority must send the Appropriations Committees a semiannual report of amounts transferred and purposes; that report does not replace existing notification rules.
- **Sec. 503 (environmental justice):** Prohibits using any funds in the Act in contravention of Executive Order 12898 (Federal Actions to Address Environmental Justice in Minority Populations and Low-Income Populations). It does not create a new program or appropriate money for environmental justice work.

## Plain English

This title does not spend new money; it tells agencies they cannot use these appropriations to lobby Congress, shuffle title III funds outside approved transfer rules, or act contrary to the federal environmental-justice order.
